name: Pattern 2: The Human Review Gate
title: Pattern 2: The Human Review Gate
answer: The Human Review Gate is a rule that keeps certain decisions in human hands: AI may inform a decision but never make it. It matters because some choices, such as grades, services, discipline and placement, carry real consequences for students and families, and a person must remain accountable for them.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern is not a way of using AI but a limit placed on it. A defined set of decisions must pass through a gate where a person makes the call, with AI allowed only to supply information. The book lists grades, special education services, discipline, course placement, teacher evaluation, safety flags and hiring as decisions that belong behind that gate. Each school is expected to write its own version of the list and publish it, so that everyone knows which choices stay with people. The problem it solves is the quiet drift toward letting a system's output settle matters that should be settled by professional judgement.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The gate looks different at each stage of schooling. In the early grades it usually stands in front of screening, so when a reading screener flags a kindergartner as at risk for dyslexia, a teacher and a specialist examine the child before any decision is made or anything is said to the family. In middle school the gate most often protects grades, because AI can suggest a score on a quiz but cannot post it. In high school it matters most for discipline, where an AI detection score is never treated as proof that a student cheated. In every case the person behind the gate is the one who decides.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support and cites a specific warning. Research on human review finds that when a machine makes the first call, people tend to go along with it, even when it is wrong (Krugel et al., 2023). The proposed fix follows from that finding: the person should look at the evidence first and treat the AI's suggestion as a second opinion rather than the starting point. The book also notes that Chapter 3 turns this into a written rule with a list of decisions every board can adopt.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A gate only works if the person behind it forms a real opinion, which is why the order of review matters and why the human should see the evidence before the AI's suggestion. The limits are set by the school's own published list of gated decisions, and the choices that stay with a person are grades, special education services, discipline, course placement, teacher evaluation, safety flags and hiring. AI is permitted to inform these decisions but never to make them, and an AI detection score is never proof of cheating. The decisions themselves remain with the people the school holds responsible.
